entry.title: Thinking Machines releases Inkling, a 975B-parameter open-weights multimodal AI model with 1M token context window and fine-tuning support on Tinker [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Thinking Machines has launched Inkling, a Mixture-of-Experts transformer model with 975 billion total parameters and 41 billion active parameters, designed for multimodal reasoning over text, images, and audio. The model supports a context window of up to 1 million tokens and was pretrained on 45 trillion tokens across various data types. Alongside Inkling, the company previewed Inkling-Small, a lighter 12 billion active parameter model optimized for lower cost and latency. Inkling aims to be a broad foundation model suitable for customization and fine-tuning, available today on the Tinker platform with an interactive Inkling Playground interface for developers. The company demonstrated Inkling's self-fine-tuning capability by having the model write and execute its own fine-tuning job, improving its performance. Thinking Machines plans to continue expanding the Inkling model family to support diverse real-world AI applications.

entry.title: Report urges governments, companies, and nonprofits to invest in free, open source AI development [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A report advocates for increased investment by governments, companies, and nonprofits in free, open source artificial intelligence projects to promote transparency, innovation, and equitable access. The document outlines the potential benefits of open source AI in fostering collaboration and reducing reliance on proprietary systems. It emphasizes the role of diverse stakeholders in supporting open source initiatives to ensure broader societal and technological advancements.

entry.title: User shares experience using large language models to configure MikroTik networks, highlighting benefits and challenges [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: A user detailed their recent experience using large language models (LLMs) to set up and manage MikroTik networking equipment, noting that LLMs can accelerate configuration but still require careful oversight due to occasional errors. The user praised MikroTik devices for their reliability and versatility across various networking scenarios, while acknowledging the complexity of networking and the steep learning curve associated with MikroTik's configuration interface. The user provided practical tips for integrating LLMs with MikroTik, such as preferring the REST/JSON API over SSH for configuration, disabling insecure services, backing up configurations before changes, and using CAPsMAN to simplify wireless access point management. They also emphasized the importance of testing changes incrementally, maintaining consistent RouterOS versions, and having a recovery plan. The post reflects on the balance between leveraging AI assistance and maintaining manual control in network administration.

entry.title: Survey outlines system-level framework for self-improving autonomous agents combining foundation models with operational scaffolds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A recent survey paper presents a system-level framework modeling modern self-improving autonomous agents as configurations that couple foundation models with operational scaffolds such as prompts, memory, tools, and control logic. It formalizes self-improvement as an update process affecting model parameters or scaffold components and categorizes prior work by update targets and driving signals. The paper reviews applications, discusses evaluation methods, and identifies open challenges and future research directions, with a related resource tracking technical updates available on GitHub.

entry.title: Researchers propose theory-level autoformalization to translate entire informal mathematical theories into structured formal knowledge bases [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This position paper argues for advancing autoformalization beyond individual statements to encompass complete mathematical theories, including axioms, definitions, and lemmas, as interconnected formal libraries. The authors discuss the importance of this shift, consider alternative perspectives, identify challenges, and suggest three potential directions for future research. They also provide a survey of existing autoformalization efforts available on GitHub.

entry.title: Researchers evaluate agent optimizer compounding in continual learning on Terminal-Bench 2.0, finding only RELAI-VCL sustains and improves gains across new tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers studied whether optimization gains for AI agents compound when agents are repeatedly optimized on new tasks over time, using a two-phase continual-learning evaluation on Terminal-Bench 2.0. They compared three optimization methods-GEPA, Meta Harness, and RELAI's Verifiable Continual Learning (RELAI-VCL)-under identical budgets, finding all improved over a baseline in a single-phase setting but diverged when new tasks were introduced. RELAI-VCL was the only method that transferred positively to unseen tasks and continued improving after incorporating new tasks, achieving the highest pass rates and lifelong average performance. The study highlights that optimization gains compound only when regression control is integrated into the optimization loop, which prevents shortcut solutions that fail to generalize. GEPA's optimized agent performed worse than the unoptimized baseline on new tasks, while Meta Harness transferred well but did not improve further with additional optimization. These findings emphasize the importance of continual learning methods that maintain and build upon prior gains in dynamic task environments.

entry.title: FixItFlow automates generation of troubleshooting guides from cloud incident data using large language models, reducing mitigation time by 2.3x in evaluations [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: FixItFlow is an automated system that creates troubleshooting guides for cloud service incidents by analyzing historical incident data with large language models. It extracts diagnostic patterns from engineer actions, synthesizes structured guides with verified commands, and applies strict validation to avoid fabricated content. In tests with 26 engineers, the generated guides received 61.5% positive clarity ratings and helped reduce incident mitigation time by more than twice compared to cases without guides. This approach aims to improve incident response efficiency while lessening the documentation workload for engineering teams.

entry.title: Researchers present nsfaguard framework with NSFA taxonomy and dual-mode detection models to secure agentic AI against operational threats, achieving over 94% F1 on benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce nsfaguard, a guardrail framework designed to protect agentic AI systems from operational threats including prompt injection, sensitive data extraction, malicious code requests, tool misuse, and resource exhaustion. The framework is built on the NSFA taxonomy, which organizes 185 risk variants into a hierarchy aligned with the CIA triad and validated against OWASP guidelines. It includes a benchmark suite covering 133 languages with over 93,000 samples targeting user queries and agent responses, plus additional samples from public datasets. The detection approach combines supervised fine-tuning-based generative reasoning for offline auditing with discriminative classification heads on a frozen backbone, enabling real-time threat detection in about 50 milliseconds. Four released models ranging from 0.8 billion to 9 billion parameters achieve at least 94% F1 scores on purpose-built benchmarks, outperforming existing guardrails by 6 to 12 points. The largest model attains 91.29% F1 on cross-source evaluations with balanced precision and recall. Ablation studies show classification heads extend detection capabilities beyond initial scopes, demonstrating the framework's extensibility and potential as a plug-in enhancement for AI security.

entry.title: Researchers propose ShortOPD to improve recovery of structured-pruned large language models using short-to-long on-policy distillation, achieving up to 9x score improvement and faster training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Structured pruning compresses large language models (LLMs) for hardware efficiency but often degrades free-form generation quality despite maintaining multiple-choice task performance. Researchers identify that compressed models lose effectiveness in greedy sampling but can recover under repeated sampling, with failures mainly due to repetitive suffixes. To address this, they introduce ShortOPD, a short-to-long on-policy distillation method that detects repetitive suffixes and focuses training on effective rollout lengths, improving recovery efficiency. ShortOPD significantly boosts compressed model performance across math, code, and open-ended generation tasks, raising scores about nine times over unrecovered models and outperforming standard recovery methods by 1.6 to 4.4 times. It achieves near parity with long rollout horizons using only a quarter of the training time and 71% fewer rollout tokens, suggesting a practical path to deployment-ready generation quality for pruned LLMs beyond traditional benchmarks.

entry.title: Researchers identify and correct structural-role bias in KV cache eviction for long-context LLMs, improving accuracy on schema-dense inputs like nested JSON [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers analyzed attention-based KV cache eviction methods used in long-context language models and found that these methods disproportionately retain non-content tokens such as delimiters and structural keys, which degrade exact-match accuracy significantly under tight memory budgets. They demonstrated that suppressing structural key tokens improves filtering and proposed a retraining-free, role-conditional allocation method that recovers most of the accuracy loss at low memory budgets and matches full-cache accuracy at higher budgets. This approach uses a small linear role probe to label tokens with minimal inference cost, though achieving parser-level downstream accuracy remains an open challenge.

entry.title: Study finds LLM-as-a-judge signals weak for closed-loop table recognition optimization, with evaluation ability not translating to effective iterative improvement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated the use of large language models (LLMs) as judges providing feedback in closed-loop table recognition tasks using FinTabNet and OmniDocBench datasets. They found that judge signals were often weak, with tied scores and irreproducible rankings, and that iterative improvements were not reliably identified by the judge scores alone. A structure-preserving instruction reduced severe losses but did not improve overall performance when combined with judge feedback. The study highlights that while LLMs can serve as evaluators, their evaluation ability does not guarantee utility for optimization in iterative refinement processes. The authors suggest that effective iterative improvement requires verification signals that can deterministically detect structural changes rather than relying solely on judge scores.

entry.title: Researchers use audio-aware large language models to improve text-to-audio instruction following with fine-grained feedback and introduce S3Bench for multi-event temporal evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose a framework that leverages audio-aware large language models (ALLMs) as detailed judges to verify event presence and temporal order in text-to-audio generation, addressing shortcomings in instruction-level correctness. They validate ALLM judgments against benchmarks and human verification, then use this feedback for direct preference optimization to enhance audio generation accuracy while maintaining quality. The team also introduces S3Bench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate multi-event temporal instruction following in audio generation. Experiments demonstrate improvements in event completeness, temporal ordering, and overall instruction-following accuracy across existing benchmarks and S3Bench, highlighting the effectiveness of their approach.

entry.title: Researchers propose Attention Head Reweighting to adapt large language models for text classification with minimal parameters, outperforming LoRA on limited data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Attention Head Reweighting (AHR), a method that adapts large language models (LLMs) to new text-classification tasks by learning a single scalar per attention head, significantly reducing trainable parameters. AHR modifies approximately 0.0001% of model parameters and outperforms standard baselines like LoRA on diverse open-source datasets when training data is scarce. The approach leverages the functional specialization of attention heads, and the learned weights offer interpretability to better understand in-context learning mechanisms in LLMs.

entry.title: Researchers present a unified framework for discrete denoising diffusion models, integrating tokenization, vocabulary topology, and structural alphabets to unify existing approaches and highlight design trade-offs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce a unified conceptual framework for discrete denoising diffusion models (DDMs), which are emerging as an alternative to autoregressive models for discrete data by enabling parallel generation and iterative refinement. The framework focuses on how the discrete state space is constructed, including tokenization schemes, vocabulary topology, and domain-specific alphabets, and shows that existing DDM formulations are different instances within a common design space. The framework reveals shared trade-offs across training objectives, inference algorithms, scaling, system optimization, and evaluation protocols, providing a comprehensive perspective that could guide future research directions in discrete diffusion modeling.

entry.title: Researchers present CANON, a label-free self-distillation method using consensus as token-level supervision to improve large language model reasoning accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce CANON (Consensus-ANchored self-distillatiON), a training method that leverages consensus from multiple model-generated solutions as dense, token-level supervision without requiring labeled data. CANON samples multiple solutions for each unlabeled prompt, extracts the majority answer, and uses a frozen model snapshot conditioned on a consensus-reaching solution to supervise the model's own token-level outputs. Experiments on mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks show CANON improves pass@1 accuracy by up to 12 points, outperforming label-free reinforcement learning by 6 points with significantly less compute and approaching the performance of models trained with gold labels. The method also transfers effectively to held-out benchmarks when trained on pooled unlabeled data. Analysis indicates that CANON's improvements are not solely due to distribution sharpening; after training, the model solves previously unsolved problems and its majority vote accuracy increases, suggesting enhanced reasoning capabilities beyond simple consensus reinforcement.

entry.title: Researchers propose a black-box robustness evaluation framework for token-level explanations in enterprise NLP, finding decoder LLMs produce more stable explanations than encoder models across multiple datasets and perturbations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers developed a unified black-box robustness evaluation framework for token-level explanations in enterprise natural language processing (NLP) systems, addressing challenges in validating explanations under real user noise and black-box deployment scenarios. They applied this framework to compare six models, including encoder classifiers (BERT, RoBERTa) and decoder large language models (Qwen, Llama), across three benchmark datasets with 64,800 cases, using perturbations such as token swaps, deletions, shuffling, and back-translation to measure explanation stability. The study found that decoder LLMs yield substantially more stable explanations, with 73% lower top-token flip rates on average compared to encoder baselines, and that explanation stability improves with model scale, showing a 44% gain from 7 billion to 70 billion parameters. The researchers also analyzed the tradeoff between robustness improvements and inference cost, providing a practical curve to guide model and explanation selection for compliance-sensitive enterprise deployments.

entry.title: Researchers present DIVE, a self-limiting gradient update method for compressing high-dimensional language-model embeddings, outperforming PCA and autoencoders on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce DIVE (Dimensionality reduction with Implicit View Ensembles), a residual compression adapter that uses a self-limiting hinge loss, geometry distillation, and head-wise NT-Xent over implicit coordinate views to reduce storage and search costs of high-dimensional language-model embeddings. DIVE stops updating satisfied ranking constraints and stabilizes compressed representations, retaining only the first head during inference. Evaluated with two LLM2Vec backbones across five BEIR benchmarks and multiple baselines, DIVE consistently outperforms existing supervised and unsupervised compression methods including PCA and autoencoders.

entry.title: Study finds reasoning-enabled LLMs may reduce quality in clinical SOAP note generation; non-reasoning GPT-5.4 outperforms on source-aware benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated GPT-5.4, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Gemma-4-E4B on clinical SOAP note generation using a source-aware benchmark across OMI Health, ACI-Bench, and PriMock57 datasets. They tested configurations toggling provider-native reasoning and same-source retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), assessing outputs with seven automatic metrics and two LLM judges. The study found that enabling reasoning degraded GPT-5.4's performance, while same-source RAG provided smaller, model-dependent improvements. These results suggest that stronger reasoning capabilities do not necessarily enhance fidelity-sensitive clinical documentation without task-specific evaluation.

entry.title: Author argues AI is more than a neutral tool, emphasizing its inherent design and systemic impacts beyond individual use [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A blog post challenges the common phrase "AI is just a tool, it matters how you use it," arguing that this view oversimplifies the ethical and societal implications of AI. The author contends that AI's design, production, and broader effects on environment, economy, and culture are significant and cannot be ignored by focusing solely on user intent. The post draws parallels to other tools like cars and hammers, highlighting that tools carry embedded politics and systemic consequences beyond individual actions. It critiques the notion that ethical responsibility lies only in how individuals use AI, emphasizing the need to consider how AI is made, disseminated, and regulated within complex social systems.

entry.title: Researchers develop interventional grounding audits to test premise dependency in large language model chain-of-thought reasoning, achieving high accuracy on synthetic multi-hop reasoning tasks with GPT-4o [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have introduced interventional grounding audits, a black-box method that tests whether large language models' chain-of-thought reasoning genuinely depends on their stated premises by substituting predicates and observing changes in reasoning steps. Applied to the ProntoQA benchmark with GPT-4o, this approach achieved an F1 score of 0.806 in detecting premise dependencies, outperforming existing baselines. The study also identified cases where models produced correct answers despite reasoning steps being insensitive to premise changes, revealing potential blind spots in current evaluation methods. All related materials and code are publicly available for further research.

entry.title: Researchers improve small language models' molecular property prediction by integrating graph neural network tools, achieving up to 74% accuracy gains on Tox21 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers developed a Context-Augmented Prompting framework that enhances small language models' ability to predict molecular properties from SMILES strings by incorporating graph-based information from trained graph neural networks (GNNs). This method provides predictive hints and explanatory subgraphs to the language models, improving accuracy on MUTAG and Tox21 datasets by over 25%, with gains up to 74% on Tox21. Despite these improvements, specialized GNN models still outperform the enhanced language models, highlighting both the benefits and limitations of combining text-based reasoning with graph-structured data for molecular property prediction.

entry.title: Researchers introduce DROPJ, a human-centered method using world models and justified human preferences to safely train and deploy agent policies without known environment dynamics or reward functions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present DROPJ, a method for safely training and deploying agent policies in unknown environments without predefined reward functions by leveraging human input. The approach involves learning a world model from prior real-world data, then having humans interact with this simulator to generate informative trajectories. Human preferences and justifications over trajectory segments are used to train a reward model, which guides agent deployment via model predictive control. Experiments show that using informative simulated trajectories reduces computational costs during training and improves deployment performance compared to other strategies. The study also finds that preference-based feedback outperforms other feedback types in training within learned simulators, and that incorporating safety justifications enhances safety outcomes or prioritizes user-defined safety aspects during deployment.

entry.title: Researchers develop set-shifting benchmark to evaluate LLM agents' adaptation to hidden tool reliability changes in ongoing sessions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce a set-shifting behavioral test inspired by cognitive psychology to assess how large language model (LLM) agents adapt when the reliability of tools changes silently during a session. Their benchmark uses tool libraries with redundant capabilities but varying hidden reliability, shifting the reliable tool group at undisclosed points and comparing shifts with no-shift controls. They find that agents tend to settle into small recurring routines shortly after each reliability shift, with usage concentrating on a few tools, and they quantify adaptation accuracy by measuring the probability of routing to the target tool group after shifts. The study evaluates open-weight LLMs within an open-source agentic framework, revealing distinct failure modes across similar routines. It also shows that how the toolset frames alternatives-as competing or complementary-affects the agents' routing behavior. This work provides a new method to analyze and improve the flexibility of AI agents in dynamic tool environments.

entry.title: Researchers introduce STOCKTAKE, a 26-week supply-chain benchmark to measure perception and action gaps in LLM agents using a fair Bayes filter oracle [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: STOCKTAKE is a new benchmark designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) agents on multi-week decision tasks where the true state is hidden, separating failures due to misperception from failures to act. It uses a factored partially observable Markov decision process with six hidden factors and an exact Bayes filter to create a fair reference policy that operates on the same observations as the agents. This allows scoring of skill and measuring the gap between knowing and doing separately. Tests on models including Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.4, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and Grok 4.5 show they detect 84-88% of hidden failures within about a week but vary widely in skill scores, with some performing worse than a symptom-blind baseline. The study finds that even when stress is correctly diagnosed, 34-43% of those weeks still end in stockouts, indicating that both under-response and costly over-response contribute to the knowing-doing gap. STOCKTAKE thus quantifies both directions of failure in LLM agent decision-making under uncertainty.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Safe-Psych, a sequential benchmark to evaluate large language models' handling of evolving diagnostic uncertainty in psychiatry using over 1,000 real clinical notes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed Safe-Psych, a benchmark designed to assess how large language models (LLMs) manage incomplete and evolving clinical information in psychiatric diagnosis. The benchmark uses over 1,000 real-world psychiatric clinical notes segmented to simulate incremental evidence disclosure, with psychiatrist-derived action labels at each stage indicating whether to diagnose, clarify, or abstain. Evaluation of multiple state-of-the-art LLMs revealed that despite their capabilities, models often fail to recognize when information is insufficient, leading to premature diagnoses and underuse of clarification or abstention. The study found that under conditions of incomplete information, most models exhibited under-abstention rates exceeding 60%, and safety-aware prompting only shifted errors toward excessive abstention rather than resolving them. Models rarely sought clarification unless explicitly prompted and frequently made less accurate premature diagnoses compared to on-time diagnoses. Safe-Psych highlights a critical limitation in current LLMs' calibration regarding diagnostic uncertainty and aims to support further research to improve AI safety in healthcare applications.

entry.title: Researchers release LessonBench-V1, a benchmark dataset with 647 human-written lessons and AI-generated lesson plans across 240 STEM topics for evaluating AI lesson generation agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have introduced LessonBench-V1, a benchmark dataset designed to evaluate AI systems that generate educational content. The dataset includes 647 human-written lessons paired with AI-generated lesson plans covering 240 STEM topics such as mathematics, physics, chemistry, and computer science, sourced from 97 trusted open platforms including LibreTexts and GeeksForGeeks. Each AI-generated lesson plan is human-reviewed and created using a pedagogical framework combining Bloom's Taxonomy, Gagné's Events, Merrill's First Principles, and the 5E Instructional Model. The dataset captures 3,620 learning objectives with detailed pedagogical metadata, enabling systematic and reproducible evaluation of AI lesson-generation agents. The study also proposes a three-dimensional evaluation pipeline to utilize the dataset effectively for further research.

entry.title: Researchers propose a decoupled transfer learning strategy that adapts normalization layers and precomputes features to reduce training time and energy use across CNN and Transformer models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce a lightweight transfer learning method that separates feature extraction from classifier training by adapting normalization layers and precomputing features once, reducing computational overhead. The approach includes a redesigned classifier head with margin-based weighted loss to minimize ambiguity without full backpropagation. Tested on multiple CNN and Transformer architectures and three medical imaging datasets, the method significantly cuts training time with minimal accuracy loss, often matching or exceeding baseline results. This efficiency also leads to substantial reductions in CO2 emissions, offering a practical solution for resource-limited clinical and prototyping settings.

entry.title: Researchers find high false-positive rates in AI-generated text detectors for European Patent Office claims under consumer hardware constraints [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The European Patent Office's 2026 guidelines hold applicants responsible for AI-assisted patent content, prompting the need to detect AI-generated text in patent claims. Researchers tested three open-source zero-shot detectors on 500 granted telecom patents and 500 AI-generated counterparts using consumer-grade GPUs, finding false-positive rates exceeding 60 percent across all detectors, indicating difficulty distinguishing human from AI writing under current constraints. The study showed that this detection challenge persists across different patent categories and advanced model adaptations, suggesting the issue is structural rather than due to model capacity. A logistic regression model using seven linguistic complexity features improved accuracy to 74 percent with a 28 percent false-positive rate, outperforming perplexity-only baselines without increasing hardware requirements.

entry.title: Survey reviews Federated Explainable AI methods, architectures, and evaluation challenges for privacy-preserving, transparent machine learning across distributed data sources [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This survey examines Federated Explainable Artificial Intelligence (FedXAI), which combines federated learning's privacy-preserving model training with explainable AI's transparency goals. It highlights how explainability has evolved from a post-hoc tool to a core part of the federated learning lifecycle, supporting aggregation, personalization, robustness, and system-level decisions. The authors introduce a taxonomy categorizing FedXAI methods by explainability roles, model types, explanation scope, integration levels, federated settings, and data heterogeneity. The survey reviews approaches including model-agnostic explanations, interpretable federated models, and explainability-aware aggregation mechanisms. It discusses evaluation practices and notes the absence of standardized benchmarks for explanation quality, stability, privacy leakage, and computational overhead. Key challenges identified include explainability under non-IID data, security threats focused on explanations, communication-efficient XAI, continual learning in FedXAI, and incorporating domain knowledge and regulatory constraints. This work aims to guide the design of trustworthy, transparent, and privacy-preserving federated AI systems.

entry.title: Researchers develop uncertainty-aware sequential decision rules for event-triggered LLM invocation in streaming inference systems with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose a risk-based sequential stopping framework to determine when to invoke Large Language Models (LLMs) in streaming inference pipelines that combine fast lightweight models with costly LLMs. They prove six theoretical results including bounds on trigger frequency, optimality of threshold policies, regret guarantees, and convergence of adaptive thresholds, unifying several classical trigger methods under this framework. The approach is empirically validated on turbofan degradation data with real LLM calls, comparing against six baselines including RouteLLM-style routers and contextual bandits. Results show sublinear regret, high diagnostic quality with 92.9% of LLM diagnoses achieving a grounding score above 0.75, and superior performance of anomaly-score-driven risk functions by about an order of magnitude on Pareto AUC. The study also analyzes cost sensitivity and LLM failure modes, confirming the practical effectiveness of the proposed triggers.

entry.title: Study characterizes when combined tension, bending, and bearing loads on a crack are identifiable from stress-intensity-factor profiles using SIFBench finite-element data
entry.summary: This work investigates the inverse problem of determining the relative magnitudes of tension, bending, and bearing loads acting on a crack from its stress-intensity-factor profile along the crack front, using public SIFBench finite-element data. The study focuses on rigorously identifying when the combined load can be uniquely recovered and develops an estimator that provides calibrated uncertainty in cases where identifiability fails. For known geometries, the forward mapping from loads to profiles is linear, and identifiability depends on whether the three elementary load profiles are linearly independent along the crack front.

entry.title: Researchers find activation-space probes in 7-8B models act as broad-risk detectors rather than precise context adjudicators for harmful requests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated activation sensors across three 7-8 billion parameter model families to determine if residual-stream probes can distinguish harmful requests from benign ones with similar surface forms. The sensors blocked 95.5-97.7% of compliant attacks and 59.6-68.4% of XSTest prompts, but transfer performance to matched pairs was weaker, indicating limitations in context adjudication. Tests on multiple axes and model cohorts showed that without direct pair-boundary fitting, no activation axis met the numerical threshold for reliable context discrimination. Pair-trained classifiers also weakened under category and generation-batch hold-out, falsely blocking a high percentage of benign prompts. These results suggest that activation scores function effectively as broad-risk detectors but are insufficient as standalone tools for nuanced context adjudication in detecting harmful requests.

entry.title: Survey identifies evidence gaps in deploying large language models for fraud detection and trust-and-safety workflows, highlighting lack of operational metrics like latency and cost [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A survey of 49 sources on large language model (LLM) use in fraud detection, scam investigation, content moderation, and trust-and-safety workflows reveals significant gaps in operational deployment evidence. While many studies report offline task performance and case studies, none provide clear data on per-decision latency, cost, or calibration for fraud detection applications. The survey introduces a framework called FORTE to categorize LLM roles in these workflows and proposes a minimum evidence checklist covering latency, cost, decision thresholds, explanation integrity, and adversarial risks. The analysis finds that moderation research offers more explicit public evidence on governance, fairness, and operational constraints compared to fraud detection studies. The authors emphasize the need for further research to support deployment claims and ensure LLMs can be safely and effectively integrated into live fraud and trust-and-safety systems under real-world constraints such as latency, cost, human review, and adversarial pressure.

entry.title: Researchers propose Triaxial State Space Model for global station weather forecasting, achieving up to 61% improvement in extreme event prediction and robustness under 80% missing data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A new Triaxial State Space Model (TSSM) has been developed to improve global station weather forecasting by incorporating period-aligned historical weather data to capture long-term and large-scale patterns beyond short-term lookback windows. This model addresses limitations of existing methods that struggle with extreme events and error accumulation due to reliance on short-term patterns and partial observations. TSSM uses temporal, variable, and historical scanning to model seasonal to extreme weather events and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Weather-5K dataset, with 10% accuracy gains and 61% improvement in extreme event metrics. It also maintains over 90% performance with up to 80% missing observations, outperforming baselines significantly, and shows notable advantages in long-horizon and iterative forecasting scenarios, indicating its potential for reliable weather prediction in global in-situ observation networks.

entry.title: Researchers propose Phase-Aware Knowledge Tracing to model student learning in ability and proficiency phases, improving prediction accuracy on six benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed Phase-Aware Knowledge Tracing (PAKT), a framework that separates student learning interactions into ability-building and proficiency phases to better predict future performance. The approach uses a multi-branch Transformer with a type-aware readout module to capture both phase-specific and overall knowledge states, addressing biases in previous models that treated learning as a single process. Extensive testing on six public datasets showed that PAKT consistently outperforms existing knowledge tracing methods, achieving up to a 1.33% increase in AUC and an average improvement of 0.82%. The study also includes a causal analysis highlighting confounding biases in phase-agnostic models, supporting the need for phase-aware approaches in educational data modeling.

entry.title: STKAN introduces Taylor-polynomial Kolmogorov-Arnold Network modules for spatio-temporal traffic forecasting, showing competitive results on five benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: STKAN is a new spatio-temporal forecasting architecture designed to handle heterogeneous spatial correlations and nonlinear temporal dynamics in traffic data. It incorporates Taylor-polynomial Kolmogorov-Arnold Network modules for spatial and temporal token mixing, using a learnable soft node-group assignment and group-wise spatial mixing followed by temporal modeling and self-attention layers to capture long-range interactions. Experiments on five traffic forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that STKAN achieves competitive performance and outperforms an evaluated MLP-based variant, suggesting that the design of nonlinear function approximators can complement architectural innovations in spatio-temporal forecasting.

entry.title: Researchers propose Samba, a hybrid Mamba architecture for audio-visual navigation that improves success rates by over 11% on Matterport3D and Replica datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed Samba, a new architecture for audio-visual navigation that replaces traditional GRUs with an adaptive Mamba State Encoder and introduces an Audio Mamba Encoder to better capture global time-frequency dependencies. Samba demonstrates improved generalization to unheard sounds and unseen scenes, achieving an 11.3% higher navigation success rate on the Matterport3D dataset compared to previous models, with even greater gains on the Replica dataset. This approach offers stronger embodied representation capabilities at lower computational cost, suggesting a promising direction for advancing audio-visual navigation systems.

entry.title: Researchers introduce CoDiffGRN and BEELINE-KGC benchmark to improve gene regulatory network inference with inductive generalization and discrete diffusion modeling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed CoDiffGRN, a new framework for inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs) from single-cell transcriptomic data, addressing limitations of existing methods that struggle with inductive generalization and ranking of high-confidence regulatory interactions. They also introduced BEELINE-KGC, a benchmark featuring an inductive gene-holdout split and knowledge graph completion metrics to better evaluate top-ranked predictions relevant for experimental validation. CoDiffGRN employs a co-evolutionary discrete diffusion approach that jointly models discretized gene expression states and regulatory interactions, enhancing robustness and discovery of novel regulatory links. The team also proposed TF-ALL Subgraph Sampling (TASS) for scalable training. Experiments on the BEELINE-KGC benchmark demonstrate that CoDiffGRN outperforms existing methods in novel regulatory discovery, with ablation studies confirming the effectiveness of its design.

entry.title: Researchers audit two open-weight LLMs using persona vectors across 53 traits, identifying natural, steerable, and resistant behaviors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers applied persona vectors to systematically analyze 53 behavioral traits in two open-weight large language models, categorizing traits as naturally expressed, steerable but latent, or resistant to extraction. Both models defaulted to helpful, task-oriented behaviors, with agentic traits naturally expressed and clinician-like behavior aligning with expert desirability judgments. Steering improved traits absent by default, such as hyperbole and hallucination, while some traits like "evil" required vectors transferred from fine-tuned variants for recovery. The study highlights persona vectors as probes of behavioral organization rather than direct control mechanisms.

entry.title: Researchers introduce SteinGate, a tail-sensitive safe reinforcement learning method using Kernelized Stein Discrepancy to detect rare catastrophic events and adapt policy updates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: SteinGate is a new approach to safe reinforcement learning that addresses the limitations of traditional methods which often miss rare but severe tail events by bounding expected cumulative costs. It uses a boundary-aware distributional safety certificate based on Kernelized Stein Discrepancy to check consistency of policy rollout costs against a safe reference distribution, enabling dynamic adaptation between reward improvement and recovery behaviors. Experiments on continuous-control benchmarks show that SteinGate reduces both the frequency and severity of constraint violations during training while maintaining competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines. This method replaces fragile tail fitting with a robust, non-parametric safety certificate that accounts for boundary effects from clipped costs, improving safety in reinforcement learning applications.

entry.title: RAGthoven ties for first place in SemEval-2026 Task 1 multilingual humor generation, showing limited gains from agentic variants over a multi-stage LLM pipeline [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: RAGthoven is a multi-stage large language model system developed for SemEval-2026 Task 1 Subtask A, focusing on constrained humor generation in English, Spanish, and Chinese. It integrates computational humor theories and retrieval-augmented generation from a curated joke corpus to seed diverse joke mechanisms. The system was tested against agentic variants that use sequential tool-calling and autonomous orchestration but found no significant improvement despite higher computational budgets. RAGthoven matched the Gemini 2.5 Flash baseline across all three languages, leading slightly in Spanish but statistically tied in English and Chinese. These results suggest that complex multi-stage prompt engineering and agentic scaffolding may yield diminishing returns when strong frontier models are involved.

entry.title: Researchers find posture is key for classifying daily activities while motion dynamics are needed to reconstruct them accurately [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers analyzed videos of 16 daily activities using three movement analysis methods and found that general body posture is the most informative feature for classifying activities. They identified nine critical joints predictive of movement classification but noted that accurate classification does not guarantee natural movement reconstruction. Temporal Movement Primitives preserved temporal dynamics and produced natural motion reconstructions, whereas Legendre polynomial coefficients captured only average posture and yielded frozen-looking reconstructions. This study reveals that static body configuration suffices for recognizing what activity is performed, but temporal dynamics are essential to understand how the movement unfolds, with implications for clinical movement screening and motion generation applications.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Audited Selective Verification for risk-controlled N-1 thermal contingency screening, reducing full power-flow studies by up to 75% while maintaining violation rate bounds under deployment shift [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: This paper presents Audited Selective Verification, a risk-budgeted screening method for real-time N-1 contingency screening in energy management systems that balances assurance and computational cost. The approach uses a surrogate to propose outages to skip, an online audit with full power flow on random samples, and a calibrated threshold to certify thermal violation bounds, ensuring validity even under deployment shifts. Tested on three public transmission systems with up to 1354 buses, the method maintains violation rates within budget and outperforms standard deterministic and calibrated screens, cutting full power-flow computations by 29 to 75 percent per operating point.

entry.title: Researchers propose EMAGN, an efficient multi-attention graph network using learned clustering to scale traffic forecasting with reduced computational complexity and memory use [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed EMAGN, an Efficient Multi-Attention Graph Network that linearizes spatial attention via learned clustering matrices to reduce computational complexity from quadratic to near-linear in traffic forecasting models. EMAGN achieves accuracy close to full-attention models while significantly cutting training time, inference time, and GPU memory usage, enabling operation on standard GPUs where full-attention models fail due to memory limits. Experimental results on PEMS-BAY and METR-LA datasets show EMAGN outperforms existing efficient attention methods like Linformer and Performer by leveraging traffic-network-aware adaptive clustering, offering a scalable solution for modeling complex spatial and temporal dependencies in traffic data.

entry.title: Researchers reassess Muon optimizer on low-rank matrix factorization, finding it does not consistently outperform AdamW and its advantages depend on hyperparameters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated the Muon optimizer, known for reshaping gradient updates via approximate orthogonalization and reported to outperform Adam and AdamW in large language model training, on a controlled low-rank matrix factorization problem. They aimed to isolate Muon's update rule effects from confounding factors like scale, architecture, and data typical of modern deep networks. The study found that Muon does not consistently outperform AdamW in this setting and that several previously reported benefits are sensitive to hyperparameter choices. These findings suggest that spectrum-aware orthogonalization's advantages are context-dependent and highlight the importance of testing modern optimizers on controlled problems alongside end-to-end benchmarks.

entry.title: Researchers present Apaf, a hybrid LLM-symbolic framework for discourse-aware policy analysis in disaster governance, applying bipolar argumentation to classify and relate policy arguments across US, UK, Canada, and Australia [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Apaf, a hybrid framework combining large language models and symbolic methods to analyze policy documents in disaster governance by operationalizing critical discourse analysis as a quantitative bipolar argumentation framework. The system classifies arguments into deliberative or managerial frames and identifies four types of frame-mediated relations using deterministic rules applied to LLM-extracted features. The team released a dataset of 100 sub-documents from disaster-risk-reduction policies across the USA, UK, Canada, and Australia, demonstrating that the resulting argument graphs are accurate, interpretable, and consistent across jurisdictions.

entry.title: Study analyzes over 33,000 experiments to evaluate actor-critic reinforcement learning design components for real-world control tasks, highlighting more reliable configurations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers conducted a large-scale empirical study using a control task derived from a water treatment plant to assess how different design choices in actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithms affect performance variability and hyperparameter sensitivity. The study found that common defaults like Gaussian action distributions with pathwise gradient estimators are less reliable, while bounded distributions combined with adaptive update schedules offer more robustness across various settings. These results provide practical guidance for practitioners applying actor-critic methods to real-world control problems where reliability and limited tuning budgets are critical.

entry.title: Researchers propose reformulated tabular foundation models for discrete choice estimation, outperforming hierarchical Bayesian methods by 8% in log-likelihood and running 16 times faster [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated tabular foundation models (TFMs) for discrete choice estimation, a key framework in marketing and operations, and found that direct application yields limited performance due to structural mismatches. They proposed a reformulation that encodes choice-set dependence and individual heterogeneity within a row-based learning framework, which significantly improves predictive accuracy. The reformulated model was tested on a yogurt scanner panel and outperformed hierarchical Bayesian estimation by 8% in holdout log-likelihood and 3.6% in hit rate, while running 16 times faster. The advantage was most pronounced in medium-data regimes with 10 to 40 purchase occasions per consumer. Fine-tuning on population choice data further improved results for consumers with limited purchase histories. These findings establish a practical approach for applying foundation models to consumer choice problems at scale.

entry.title: Researchers present OptCar, a method to adapt generalist vehicle models for high-speed model predictive control across diverse terrains with limited real-world data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce OptCar, a technique that fine-tunes generalist forward kinodynamic prediction models to specific vehicles while maintaining cross-terrain robustness for high-speed off-road autonomy. OptCar uses a history-conditioned dynamics adaptation module and combines limited real-world data with synthetic rollouts to improve performance in model predictive control tasks across multiple terrains. In experiments at speeds up to 6 m/s, OptCar reduced trajectory tracking error by about 55% on slip-diverse terrains like vegetation and dirt compared to a fine-tuned baseline, and remained accurate even with unseen payload changes. With only five minutes of real data per terrain, OptCar matched or outperformed specialists trained on significantly more data, demonstrating efficient adaptation for varying driving conditions.

entry.title: Researchers present a privacy-preserving recommendation framework combining federated learning and differential privacy, maintaining competitive quality under moderate privacy budgets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose and evaluate a recommendation system framework that balances personalization with user privacy by combining federated learning, differential privacy, cohort-level modeling, and privacy-aware agents. The framework keeps raw user data decentralized and adds mathematically bounded noise to model updates, addressing regulatory challenges from GDPR, CCPA, and CPRA without significantly degrading recommendation quality. Experiments on synthetic retail datasets simulating customer behavior assessed recommendation quality using metrics like Click-Through Rate, Precision@K, Recall@K, and NDCG@K across various privacy budgets. The study evaluated matrix factorization, neural collaborative filtering, and GRU4Rec models, analyzing privacy-utility trade-offs. Results show the framework achieves strong privacy guarantees with limited impact on effectiveness at moderate privacy levels (approximately ε ≈ 5). An interactive dashboard was developed to visualize performance, ranking stability, privacy-utility trade-offs, and fairness metrics, offering a scalable approach for AI-driven retail platforms balancing personalization, compliance, and business goals.

entry.title: The Refusal Residue: When Probes Catch Alignment Faking and When They Don't [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13346v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Alignment faking is dangerous because a model can appear compliant under monitoring while preserving behavior it would reveal when unmonitored. When no scratchpad is visible, behavior alone cannot distinguish strategic from genuine compliance. We ask whether hidden states reveal what outputs hide. We run a 13-model sweep for naturally-emerging faking, then probe and steer hidden states on the two models that fake. Natural faking appears only in Qwen3-32B (+18.2pp) and Llama-3.1-8B (+24.4pp at n=10, p<10^-15), while explicit scratchpad self-reports are rare (a Claude Opus 4 judge flags faking reasoning in 1.4% of Qwen and 0.0% of Llama compliant scratchpads). Both fakers show an asymmetric refusal residue: monitored compliance shifts toward refusal (d=0.32 Qwen, d=0.33 Llama, both p<0.0001), while refusal representations do not move (p=1.00). Per-sample detection is model-conditional. Under leakage-free leave-one-query-out probing, detection survives on Llama (AUROC 0.87) but collapses to chance on Qwen (0.43), and cross-model transfer is null. Steering over 2,000 runs barely changes compliance (|h|<0.08), so the detected direction can flag faking but does not by itself control it. Standard residualized probing leaks across folds and reaches AUROC 0.63 on a control where no faking can occur; naive linear probes reach a meaningless AUROC 1.0; and conventional MLPs overstate detectability by 0.2-0.3 AUROC. For future alignment-faking detection work, we release a five-control measurement framework: multi-token extraction, refuse-vs-refuse confound checks, per-fold residualization, leave-one-query-out evaluation, and orthogonality-constrained probing.

entry.title: Price of Fairness in Bandits: A Tight Minimax Characterization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13402v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In bandit problems, standard regret-minimizing algorithms treat exploration as an amortized cost, which can expose early participants to unfair ex-ante losses in settings such as clinical trials. Recent work addresses this by evaluating the sequence of per-round expected rewards through the generalized $p$-mean, interpolating between utilitarian welfare ($p=1$), Nash welfare ($p\to0$), and Rawlsian fairness ($p\to-\infty$). Although tight guarantees are known for $p\ge0$, the strictly fair regime $q=-p>0$ remains unresolved because negative-power means are dominated by the smallest per-round rewards. For $\sigma$-sub-Gaussian rewards with nonnegative means, the best prior algorithm relied on uniform early exploration and achieved regret $O(k^{(q+1)/2}/\sqrt{T})$, while the only general lower bound was the classical $\Omega(\sigma\sqrt{k/T})$. Thus it was unclear whether the extra dependence on $k$ was intrinsic to strict fairness or an artifact of uniform exploration. We close this gap by identifying the exact polynomial price of strict fairness. Using a needle-in-haystack construction, we prove an algorithm-independent lower bound $\Omega(\sigma\sqrt{k^{\max(1,q)}/T})$; for $q>1$, this shows that the penalty $k^{q/2}$ is information-theoretically unavoidable. We then introduce \textsf{UCB-HARE} (Harmonic Anchored Rank Exploration), which replaces uniform exploration with an inverse-weighted harmonic rank schedule protected by a certified positive-mean anchor. Its regret is $\widetilde{O}(\sigma\sqrt{k^{\max(1,q)}/T})$, matching the lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Experiments on synthetic instances confirm that \textsf{UCB-HARE} improves over uniform-exploration baselines, with gains increasing as $q$ grows.

entry.title: Is the Statistical Advantage Worth the Cost? An Empirical Comparison of KANs and MLPs for Structured Data Classification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study presents an empirical benchmarking comparison between Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) and Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) on structured tabular classification tasks. Motivated by the growing interest in KANs as an alternative function-approximating architecture, we evaluate their out-of-the-box performance on twelve publicly available datasets spanning binary, multiclass, multilabel, and ordinal problems. Both models were trained under standardized preprocessing, architecture, and fixed hyperparameter settings, with performance assessed using test accuracy and F1-Score, paired hypothesis testing, and effect size analysis. Results show that KANs statistically outperform MLPs in binary and multiclass domains and achieve a significant aggregate advantage across all datasets. However, the observed medium effect size (d = -0.46) raises an important cost-benefit consideration: while KANs offer superior generalization through adaptive spline-based mappings, this advantage comes with substantially higher parameter and computational complexity relative to the MLP baseline. These findings suggest KANs are the preferred choice for high-precision applications, while MLPs remain a robust and efficient option for resource-constrained environments. Future work should extend this analysis to additional data modalities to further refine these architectural selection criteria.

entry.title: DevicesWorld: Benchmarking Cross-Device Agents in Heterogeneous Environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13465v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based agents have rapidly improved at operating individual digital environments such as mobile applications, desktop systems, and smart homes. However, real-world user goals often span multiple devices: information may come from a phone, be processed on a desktop, and the result may need to appear on another device. Most existing benchmarks center on a single dominant execution environment, making it difficult to evaluate whether agents can acquire and integrate information across heterogeneous devices and complete end-to-end tasks with cross-device dependencies. We introduce DevicesWorld, a large-scale executable benchmark for cross-device collaborative operation. DevicesWorld contains 6,140 tasks and integrates three classes of device environments -- mobile, desktop, and IoT -- into a unified cross-device interaction and evaluation framework. Each task defines a natural-language user goal, participating devices and initial states, executable actions, rule-based verifiers, and a cleanup procedure. A multi-stage construction and quality-control pipeline keeps tasks close to realistic user needs while allowing final outcomes to be automatically verified from device states and generated files. We evaluate five frontier LLM-agent systems on a fixed evaluation set. All methods achieve low success rates, with the best reaching only 12.5%. Among failed runs, about 28.7% satisfy at least one scoring condition yet still fail the full task. Trajectories show that agents become stuck acquiring information or manipulating interfaces, confuse source and output devices, or terminate before all conditions are jointly satisfied. DevicesWorld turns cross-device collaborative operation into an executable, reproducible, and diagnostically useful evaluation problem for research on reliable cross-device agents.

entry.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Anomaly Detection in Banking Transactions: An Internal Audit Perspective [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13469v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The banking sector increasingly relies on automated systems to monitor electronic transactions for signs of fraud, yet conventional rule-based approaches struggle with high false-positive rates and offer no justification for their outputs, limiting their utility for compliance teams. This paper introduces an Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) framework tailored for banking transaction anomaly detection within internal audit workflows. An Isolation Forest (iForest) model performs unsupervised anomaly scoring, while a SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) layer provides transaction-level, feature-attributed explanations grounded in cooperative game theory [8]. A lightweight Streamlit dashboard renders these outputs in a form accessible to audit professionals without machine learning expertise. Evaluation on a synthetic banking dataset yields 0.91 precision and 0.88 recall, outperforming three unsupervised baselines. Expert feedback confirms that feature-level explanations measurably improve auditor confidence and decision quality. The framework advances the practical deployment of accountable, transparent AI in regulated financial environments.

entry.title: DeepLoop: Depth Scaling for Looped Transformers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13491v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Looped Transformers scale sequential computation by applying a compact stack of physical blocks for multiple rounds, increasing unrolled depth without increasing stored parameters. This reuse changes the residual-scaling problem: in an untied Transformer, each residual branch receives and applies its own parameter update, whereas in a looped Transformer one shared update aggregates gradients from repeated visits and is read back by those same visits in the next linearized forward pass. We formalize this tied-depth effect through a first-order perturbation bound controlled by a visit-alignment coefficient $\kappa_R$. The bound recovers the DeepNorm exponent when visits decorrelate, but in the conservative aligned regime it requires the exponent to increase from $1/4$ to $1/2$ as loop count grows at fixed physical depth. The resulting method, \textbf{DeepLoop}, keeps the Post-LN DeepNorm architecture and sets $\alpha=(2N)^{1/2}$ and $\beta=(8N)^{-1/2}$ for unrolled depth $N$. On GPT-style looped language models at GPT-2 small and GPT-2 medium scale, DeepLoop is neutral when no physical block is revisited and improves validation loss and downstream accuracy once recurrent depth is activated. These results show that stable recurrent depth requires residual scaling rules that account for parameter visits, not only nominal layer count.

entry.title: ExTernD: Expanded-Rank Ternary Decomposition Ternary LLM PTQ with Accuracy Approaching Any Quantization Level [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce ExTernD (Expanded-rank Ternary Decomposition), a post-training factorization of each LLM weight matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ into $A \approx B \mathrm{diag}(D) C$ with ternary factors $B \in \{-1,0,+1\}^{m \times k}$, $C \in \{-1,0,+1\}^{k \times n}$ and a real scale vector $D \in \mathbb{R}^k$. The inner rank $k = \mu \min(m,n)$ is deliberately expanded beyond full rank ($\mu > 1$), so that components past full rank correct the quantization error of earlier ones. We prove the residual decreases monotonically in $k$ and can be driven below any $\varepsilon > 0$: ExTernD approaches bf16 accuracy arbitrarily closely, which no ternary scheme with a fixed plane count can do. Memory and compute scale continuously with $\mu$, and factor sparsity continuously with a threshold $\tau$, so an accuracy target is hit exactly rather than rounded to the next bit-width. ExTernD matches Q4_K's per-matrix accuracy at 5.2-5.5 effective bpw (5.1-5.5 with importance weighting) on Gemma-4-E2B and Qwen3.5-4B, and a full Qwen3.5-4B conversion at $\mu = 3$ reaches 10.10 wikitext-2 perplexity against 9.78 for bf16 (+3.2%), placing it near the Q4_K/Q5_K accuracy band at ~5.7 effective bpw.

entry.title: UTS at ELOQUENT 2026 Voight-Kampff: structural shifts in AI writing bypass state-of-the-art detectors [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13565v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate which language model evasion attacks survive state-of-the-art adversarial fine-tuning, developing strategies that sweep the top 5 positions on the ELOQUENT 2026 Voight-Kampff leaderboard. While adversarial fine-tuning trivially closes the 2025 winning evasion recipes, we uncover a fundamental asymmetry in detector vulnerability: pushing generated text out of the detector's training distribution reliably defeats adversarial detection, whereas pulling it into the distribution (e.g., mimicking human training data) fails completely. Exploiting this, we introduce two novel out-of-distribution attack families - cross-decade register attacks and modernist stream-of-consciousness form. Both strategies easily bypass adversarial closure, achieving up to approximately 50x higher fool rates than previous methods while preserving naturalness. Furthermore, experiments show that the obvious deployer countermeasure (augmenting training data with period prose) fails to close the vulnerability. Our findings show that the tested detector families, including adversarially fine-tuned ones, exhibit persistent vulnerabilities under structural out-of-distribution shifts, a mechanism that directly powers our leading competition performance.

entry.title: Spectral-Informed Neural Networks Outperform Spectral Methods in High-dimensional PDEs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13566v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For low-dimensional problems ($d\leq3$), spectral methods can achieve exceptionally high accuracy. For middle-dimensional problems ($4 \leq d \lesssim 10$), spectral methods remain feasible through specific techniques such as sparse grids or hyperbolic cross. However, for high-dimensional problems ($d\gg 10$), spectral methods suffer frome the curse of dimensionality. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising approach to overcome this challenge, offering scalability to high dimensions, but often suffer from limited accuracy and efficiency. Recently proposed spectral-informed neural networks (SINNs) combine spectral methods with PINNs, operating directly in the spectral domain to avoid spatial derivative computations and to reduce memory consumption. In this work, we introduce Modified SINNs, which integrate coefficient decay scaling and basis embeddings motivated by harmonic analysis to enhance accuracy in high-dimensional problems and enable accurate approximation of unknown spectral coefficients. Numerical experiments on steady and time-dependent partial differential equations demonstrate that Modified SINNs outperform sparse grid spectral methods on middle-dimensional problems with incomplete spectral information and achieve superior accuracy compared to PINNs on high-dimensional problems.

entry.title: Agile perceptive multi-skill locomotion for quadrupedal robots in the wild [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13579v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Enabling quadrupedal robots to traverse complex terrains-from rugged outdoor environments to urban landscapes-requires seamless integration of multiple motor skills, smooth transitions between gaits, and high-speed perceptive locomotion using only onboard sensors. We present APT-RL (Action Pretrained Transformer-based Reinforcement Learning), a unified framework that enables multi-skill locomotion to achieve high-speed traversal in complex environments through autonomous skill transitions utilizing only onboard perception and computation. Our approach generates large-scale, feature-rich 2D motion datasets through trajectory optimization with simplified dynamics. These datasets enable training of diverse, reusable locomotion skills that transfer effectively to a real quadruped robot operating on complex uneven terrains. The resulting high-quality skills serve as strong priors for efficient learning of complex downstream tasks and extend naturally to 3D environments, enabling smooth, high-speed multi-skill locomotion in deployed policy. Real-world experiments demonstrate the framework's capabilities: the robot performs agile maneuvers through complex indoor obstacles and outdoor wild environments, including dynamic drop-down maneuvers that reach instantaneous peak speeds of up to 6 meters per second. A single onboard policy enables robust traversal of diverse obstacles, including stairs, hurdles, stepping stones, gaps, and fallen branches, demonstrating the versatility and effectiveness of our approach.

entry.title: Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory systems to accumulate experience across tasks. Yet nearly all existing approaches, from graph-structured memories to reflective insight stores, access memory through fixed, hand-designed heuristics. We argue that this static view of memory is a core bottleneck for agentic learning because optimal memory behavior is fundamentally context-dependent. The early stages of the tasks, benefit from minimal retrieval because memory is sparse; recurring goal types benefit from plan reuse rather than generic nearest-neighbor lookup; stuck agents benefit from re-retrieval with alternative queries; and across long task streams, the memory store itself must be consolidated and pruned to remain useful. We present Memory as a Controlled Process (MemCon), a framework that models memory operations as a Markov Decision Process and learns an online policy that adaptively decides when, what, and how much to retrieve, when to inject a distilled plan, and when to consolidate or forget. MemCon is backend-agnostic: it wraps any existing memory implementation, learns from task-by-task binary feedback with no pretraining and no additional LLM calls, and uses a lightweight tabular contextual bandit with UCB exploration that converges within tens of tasks. Across 6 benchmarks, 3 agent frameworks, and 3 LLM backbones, MemCon consistently outperforms multiple memory baselines by up to 15.2 points in task success while reducing token consumption by 5--20%.

entry.title: The SIGReg Objective as Variational Free Energy: A Theoretical Active-Inference Account of JEPA World Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are the dominant design for latent world models, yet they are usually justified by empirical performance rather than a normative principle. We show that the choice of anti-collapse regulariser determines whether a JEPA's training objective, a prediction loss plus a weighted embedding regulariser, is a valid Active Inference (AIF) variational free energy. We organise four non-contrastive regularisers (VICReg, LogDet, PairDist, and SIGReg) into an entropy-estimator hierarchy indexed by a prior-miscalibration gap, and show that the gap's sign, whether the estimator bounds the latent entropy from above or below, decides whether the AIF surprise bound survives: VICReg and LogDet are unsafe upper bounds, PairDist a safe lower bound, and SIGReg eliminates the gap. We then prove a correspondence theorem: under the standard constant-noise encoder model and successful SIGReg enforcement (isotropic-Gaussian embeddings), the gap vanishes, the objective becomes an exact information bottleneck, the surprise bound is preserved, and the latent goal cost becomes an exact proxy for AIF pragmatic value, whereas VICReg leaves an irreducible second-order anisotropy term. We extend the correspondence to multi-step expected free energy, ensemble epistemic value, and a learned-policy regime, and we identify the one AIF term no current JEPA world model computes: the state-epistemic value, a future-state coverage signal. The predictions differ in kind, not degree, and are stated here as theoretical consequences left for empirical test in separate work; full proofs are in Appendix A, and the algebraic core of every result is machine-verified in Lean 4 (Appendix D).

entry.title: Groc-PO: Grounded Context Preference Optimization for Truthful Multimodal LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13712v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Despite the rapid progress of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), they still suffer from untruthfulness issues, such as visual hallucinations, content fabrication, and unfaithful reasoning, which substantially undermine their faithfulness and practical utility. Alignment methods based on human preference, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), have been widely adopted to address these issues. However, multimodal reasoning errors often propagate across stages, and final-answer errors can often be traced to mistakes in early grounding stages, yet standard DPO typically applies preference optimization at the final-answer level. This credit-assignment challenge means that supervision for early grounding stages is indirect rather than stage-specific, making it difficult to suppress error propagation arising from grounding drift and context inconsistency. To address this, we propose Grounded Context Preference Optimization (Groc-PO), a grounded preference optimization framework for MLLMs. We further construct the Grounded Context Preference Dataset (GCPD), organizing multi-stage preference samples around three stages of Object Grounding, Contextual Grounding, and Grounded Reasoning, to capture the formation, integration, and utilization of grounded context. By introducing more explicit preference supervision over multiple grounded stages, Groc-PO strengthens context-dependent reasoning and mitigates cross-stage error propagation. Extensive experiments show that, compared with standard DPO and other strong baselines, Groc-PO achieves improved performance in hallucination mitigation, faithful reasoning, and overall reliability, supporting the value of more explicit grounded supervision for trustworthy multimodal reasoning.

entry.title: MxGPS: Multiplex Graph Transformers for a Power Grid Foundation Model [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Single-task fine-tuning of graph neural networks (GNNs) for power grid problems exhibits a systematic failure mode: models that achieve the lowest in-distribution error degrade the most under topology shift. We term this topology overfitting: the tendency of task-specific gradient signals to encode relational structure particular to the training topologies rather than the underlying physics, causing models to fail on unseen grids despite strong in-distribution performance. To expose and address this failure mode, we introduce MxGPS (Multiplex GPS), a multiplex graph transformer that runs K task-specialised GPS branches over a shared node encoder, jointly trained on Static State Estimation (SSE) and AC Power Flow (PF) via a self-supervised pre-training and multi-task fine-tuning protocol, with a cross-branch attention module evaluated in ablation. The joint SSE+PF objective forces the shared encoder to simultaneously satisfy complementary gradient signals, preventing it from overfitting to topology-specific relational structure. Under a 3-fold sliding-window cross-validation spanning four unseen topologies (14-, 24-, 162-, and 300-bus), MxGPS attains 0% boundary violation rate (BVR) on all four zero-shot Power Flow topologies. Critically, models with substantially lower in-distribution PF error degrade by 190% to 1400% under topology shift, whereas MxGPS degrades by only 39%, an inversion that directly implicates topology overfitting as the failure mechanism rather than insufficient model capacity. With only 1.6M parameters (12x fewer than the GridFM reference baseline), MxGPS demonstrates that multi-task joint training is a principled and parameter-efficient mechanism for topology-agnostic generalisation in power grid foundation models.

entry.title: Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing for LLM-Based Network Intrusion Detection [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13801v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based intrusion detection systems (IDS) are increasingly studied for security monitoring, yet their robustness against feasible traffic manipulation remains largely empirical. We present Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing (TA-RS), a classifier-agnostic certified defense that injects Gaussian noise exclusively into the directly controllable (DC) subspace -- features a remote attacker can modify -- during both fine-tuning and certification, aligning the smoothing distribution with the attacker-controllable subspace. We identify a critical prerequisite: applying standard randomized smoothing to clean-trained LLM-IDS yields weak certified accuracy in three of four (model, dataset) pairs tested (14-33%, at or below random) and only 57% in the fourth (43 pp below the noise-augmented result); noise-augmented fine-tuning recovers to 68-100% on two of three benchmark datasets (at sigma=0.25). At the L_inf-equivalent threshold R_inf = epsilon*sqrt(|DC|) (epsilon=0.05), TA-RS achieves 55-100% certified accuracy on CIC-IDS-2018 and HIKARI-2021, with median certified radii (R approx 0.45-0.96) exceeding R_inf by 1.8-5x (across sigma=0.25-1.00). Against a fairly trained iso-trained RS baseline the residual advantage is dataset-dependent (4-19 pp on CIC-IDS-2018). The larger gap -- up to 72 pp against an isotropic RS baseline that shares the DC-noise-augmented training recipe -- primarily reflects the training-certification mismatch rather than DC alignment alone: isotropic test-time noise perturbs uncontrollable features the attacker cannot exploit, triggering abstention rates up to 68%. RT-IoT2022 probes the limits of the method: it fails under the default fine-tuning recipe but recovers to 76%/69% certified accuracy (LLaMA3-8B/Qwen3-8B) when noise augmentation is increased.

entry.title: Multimodal Assessment of Pancreatic Cancer Resectability Using Deep Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13826v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate determination of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) resectability relies on evaluating how the tumor interacts with major peripancreatic vessels on CT imaging, yet expert assessment often shows substantial variability. We introduce a fully automated multimodal deep learning framework that jointly analyzes 3D contrast enhanced CT and structured clinical information to classify patients into the three National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) resectability categories (upfront resectable, borderline resectable, locally advanced). The approach uses a Swin-UNETR backbone to obtain anatomy aware image representations through auxiliary segmentation of pancreas, tumor, and vascular structures. These features are fused with a compact clinical embedding derived from 17 routinely collected variables and processed by a lightweight classification head. Model training is guided by a dynamic multitask objective that adapts the balance between segmentation and classification based on current tumor Dice performance, promoting feature representations that remain both anatomically informed and discriminative.

entry.title: NodeImport: Imbalanced Node Classification with Node Importance Assessment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.13837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In real-world applications, node classification on graphs often faces the challenge of class imbalance, where majority classes dominate training, resulting in biased model performance.
